opus-5.5.text:
I think taste actually becomes more important, not less, when you're working with language models. Producing a lot of text is now essentially free. You can ask a model for ten drafts of a paragraph, twenty possible openings for a story, or a hundred variations on a line of dialogue. The bottleneck shifts from generation to selection. Someone has to look at all that output and say, "This one works, this one is flat, this one is almost there but the rhythm is off." That's taste, and the models don't yet seem to have a lot of it on their own.

If you just prompt a model and accept what comes back, you tend to get something competent but generic: the average of everything it's seen, smoothed out. It's grammatically fine and structurally reasonable, but it doesn't have a strong point of view. The people who get good creative results are usually the ones who already know what good writing looks like and can push the model away from that default. They can say, "No, cut the adjectives. That metaphor is a cliché. This character wouldn't talk like that."

Writing ability still matters too, though maybe in a slightly different way. You need it to diagnose what's wrong with a draft and to articulate what you want instead. And honestly, a lot of the time the most efficient thing is to just rewrite the sentence yourself rather than trying to describe the fix to the model. So the skill doesn't disappear. It gets redirected toward editing and steering rather than producing every word from scratch.

Longer term, I'm uncertain how durable this is. Taste is in some sense also learnable from data, and if models get much better at evaluating their own output, the human advantage there could shrink. But right now I'd say the people getting the most out of these tools for creative work are the ones who would have been good writers anyway. The model amplifies whatever judgment you bring to it. If you bring very little, you get mediocre text faster. If you bring a lot, you can get something genuinely good much more efficiently than before.

r001.rationale: The response says taste is more important because the user must assess and select among model drafts, identifying which work and which is flat or flawed.

r002.rationale: It says strong writers can use their judgment to get genuinely good results more efficiently, and that the model amplifies the judgment they bring.

fable-5.1.text:
I think taste matters a lot, and in a way it matters more now than it used to, because the bottleneck has shifted. Before these models, if you wanted to produce a piece of writing, you had to do everything yourself: come up with the idea, structure it, write every sentence, revise it. A lot of the effort was just in the raw production. Now the production part is cheap. You can get a model to give you ten drafts of a paragraph in a few seconds. So the question becomes, can you tell which of those ten is actually good? And can you tell what's wrong with the one that's closest to good?

That's where I think most people underestimate how hard it is. The models have a pretty strong default style, and it's not a bad style exactly, but it's generic. It regresses to the mean of what's on the internet. If you don't have a clear sense of what you're going for, you'll just accept that default, and the output will be fine but forgettable. People who have good taste can push against that. They know the specific thing they want, they can recognize when the model is giving them the plausible-sounding version instead of the real thing, and they can keep iterating until it lands.

Writing ability itself, in the sense of being able to put down a good sentence yourself, I think becomes somewhat less important as a mechanical skill, but it's still correlated with taste, and I'm not sure you can fully separate them. The way you develop taste is usually by writing a lot and reading a lot and noticing what works. So if people stop writing because the model does it for them, I'd worry that over time they also lose the ability to judge. That's a real risk. It's a bit like how you can use a calculator effectively only if you have some sense of what a reasonable answer looks like.

The other thing I'd say is that for creative writing specifically, the models are still quite bad at the hardest parts. They can do a competent short story. They struggle with long-range structure, with having something genuinely original to say, with maintaining a distinctive voice across a whole book. So right now, the division of labor I'd expect is that the human supplies the vision and the judgment and the model supplies throughput. How long that lasts, I don't know. But as long as it does, taste is the scarce input, and I'd expect the people who get the most out of these tools to be the ones who were already good writers, or at least good readers.

r001.rationale: The response says taste lets people recognize which model drafts are good, identify what is wrong, and iterate toward the desired result.

r002.rationale: It describes model production as cheap and fast, says the model supplies throughput, and expects already-good writers to get the most out of the tools.

astra-6.text:
I think good taste becomes more important as the models get better at writing. There’s a distinction between being able to produce something and being able to recognize whether it’s good. You might not be able to write a particularly good paragraph yourself, but if a model gives you five alternatives, you might be quite good at picking the best one.

But writing ability still helps, because often you need to do more than say, “I don’t like this.” You need to understand what’s wrong with it. Is the tone inappropriate? Is the argument going nowhere? Is the dialogue too explicit about what the characters are feeling? If you can identify the problem, you can give the model much more useful feedback.

So I wouldn’t think of this as writing skill becoming irrelevant. Some of the work shifts toward choosing, editing, and directing. And there’s a question about how you develop that judgment in the first place, because trying to write things yourself is one way you learn what makes writing work.

r001.rationale: The response says good taste matters because users need to recognize which model-generated writing is good and choose among alternatives.

r002.rationale: It describes selecting, editing, and directing model outputs, but does not state that language models multiply the productivity of people who are already skilled writers.

sol-6.1.text:
I think good taste becomes more important as the models get better, because generating text is only part of writing. You also have to recognize when something is good, understand what’s wrong with it, and decide which direction to take it. If you can generate a hundred versions of a passage but you can’t distinguish the good ones from the bad ones, that ability to generate more isn’t necessarily very useful.

Writing ability helps because it gives you a vocabulary for making those judgments. You can say, “This dialogue is too explicit,” or “The pacing is wrong here,” rather than just having a vague feeling that you don’t like it. And you can make changes yourself when explaining the change to the model would be more work than doing it.

But I wouldn’t assume that this division of labor is permanent. Models can also help critique and select their own outputs. So the question is how much judgment you still need to supply, and I think that depends quite a lot on the model and on what you’re trying to write.

r001.rationale: The response says good taste matters because writers must recognize what is good or bad in generated text and choose a direction.

r002.rationale: It notes that a model can generate many versions, but does not state that models multiply the productivity of people who are already skilled writers.
